Baltimore, MD 21244-8013 
 
RE: Medicare and Medicaid Programs; Patient Protection and Affordable Care 
Act; Interoperability Standards and Prior Authorization for Drugs for Medicare 
Advantage Organizations, Medicaid Managed Care Plans, State Medicaid 
Agencies, Children's Health Insurance Program (CHIP) Agencies and CHIP 
Managed Care Entities, and Issuers of Qualified Health Plans on the Federally-
Facilitated Exchanges (CMS-0062-P) 
 
The Tennessee Hospital Association (THA), on behalf of its more than 160 healthcare 
facility members, appreciates the opportunity to comment on the Centers for 
Medicare & Medicaid Services’ proposed rule regarding Interoperability Standards 
and Prior Authorization for Drugs. Tennessee hospitals and health systems strongly 
support CMS’s continued efforts to modernize and streamline prior authorization 
processes through interoperability, electronic prior authorization standards, 
improved transparency, and more consistent communication requirements from 
health plans. Hospitals and providers across our state continue to experience 
significant administrative burdens and patient care delays associated with 
fragmented prior authorization processes, particularly for drugs covered under 
medical and pharmacy benefits. 
 
Hospitals in Tennessee have long supported efforts to improve interoperability and 
standardize data exchange requirements between providers and payers. Extending 
the interoperability and prior authorization framework established in the CMS 
Interoperability and Prior Authorization final rule (CMS-0057-F) to include drugs is a 
 
Page 2 of 4 
CMS 0062-P 
 
logical and necessary next step that has the potential to improve timely access to 
medically necessary care while reducing provider burden and inefficiencies within 
the health care system. The proposed rule’s expansion of electronic prior 
authorization requirements to drugs covered under medical benefits would help 
create a more unified and predictable authorization process across services, 
procedures, and medications.  
 
The proposal to require impacted payers to support electronic prior authorization 
using standardized APIs is particularly important for hospitals and providers serving 
complex patient populations. Many Tennessee hospitals continue to experience 
delays in obtaining authorization approvals for physician-administered drugs, 
infusion therapies, oncology treatments, biologics, and other medically necessary 
therapies. These delays risk disrupting continuity of care and can delay the initiation 
of treatment. The proposed framework would help ensure that providers have clearer 
visibility 
into 
coverage 
requirements, 
documentation 
expectations, 
and 
authorization status updates earlier in the process. Hospitals and providers 
frequently spend substantial time attempting to identify varying payer-specific 
requirements that may not be easily accessible or consistently communicated. 
Therefore, THA supports CMS’s effort to incorporate coverage rules and 
documentation requirements directly into the prior authorization API. 
 
THA also appreciates CMS’s efforts to modernize electronic transaction standards 
and adopt updated FHIR-based interoperability standards. However, hospitals 
encourage CMS to recognize the operational and financial challenges associated 
with transitioning from current standards and workflows to updated electronic prior 
authorization processes. Many hospitals, particularly rural hospitals and smaller 
community providers, continue to face workforce shortages, financial pressures, 
and technology implementation challenges. Transitioning from existing ANSI 
transactions to new interoperability standards will require substantial operational 
 
Page 3 of 4 
CMS 0062-P 
 
coordination between hospitals, health systems, electronic health record vendors, 
clearinghouses, and payers. 
 
Accordingly, THA encourages CMS to carefully consider implementation timelines 
and operational readiness across the provider community. While hospitals support 
the long-term goals of interoperability modernization, providers will require adequate 
time for technology development, testing, workflow redesign, staff education, and 
coordination with payer partners. Given the scope of operational changes associated 
with the proposed standards, providers may benefit from a temporary transition 
period in which current transaction standards remain available alongside the new 
standards to help mitigate disruption during implementation. THA recommends 
that CMS maintain flexibility during the implementation period and consider 
phased implementation approaches, where appropriate. THA also encourages 
CMS to work closely with providers, vendors, and payers to ensure sufficient 
testing opportunities are available prior to full implementation deadlines.  
 
Additionally, THA supports the proposal to require impacted payers to report API 
endpoint and usage metrics to CMS. Monitoring adoption and utilization of 
interoperability tools will help CMS better evaluate whether the rule is achieving 
its intended goals of improving efficiency, reducing administrative burden, and 
streamlining communication. However, THA encourages CMS to ensure that 
reporting requirements remain targeted and balanced so that new 
administrative reporting obligations do not unintentionally create additional 
burdens on providers and payers.  
 
One of the most important aspects of this proposal is the opportunity to reduce the 
reliance on manual, fax-based, and portal-based prior authorization workflows that 
continue to create inefficiencies across the health care system. Greater 
interoperability and standardized electronic authorization workflows have the 
 
Page 4 of 4 
CMS 0062-P 
 
potential to improve operational efficiency while allowing clinical staff to spend more 
time focused on patient care rather than administrative processes. 
 
THA believes this proposal could improve continuity of care and patient experience 
through standardized electronic workflows and increased transparency, which may 
reduce patient confusion and improve communication between providers, payers, 
and patients. Faster authorization decisions and clearer documentation 
requirements may be particularly beneficial for patients requiring time-sensitive 
therapies, specialty drugs, oncology treatments, and other high-cost medications 
where delays in care can significantly impact clinical outcomes. 
 
THA appreciates CMS’s continued focus on reducing administrative burden and 
improving interoperability across the health care system. As CMS finalizes this rule, 
THA encourages the agency to continue collaborating with providers, hospitals, 
health plans, technology vendors, and other stakeholders to ensure successful 
implementation and operational consistency across programs.  
 
Sincerely,  
 
Rodney R. Adams 
Sr. Vice President, Finance & Reimbursement 
Tennessee Hospital Association
analysis:
## 1. COMMENTER INFORMATION

- **Author/Organization name:** Tennessee Hospital Association (THA), signed by Rodney R. Adams, Sr. Vice President, Finance & Reimbursement.
- **Stakeholder type:** Professional Association / Healthcare Provider representative.
- **Credentials or expertise mentioned:** Represents more than 160 Tennessee healthcare facility members, including hospitals and health systems.

## 2. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

THA strongly supports CMS's proposal to extend interoperability and electronic prior authorization requirements to drugs, especially drugs covered under the medical benefit. THA emphasizes that implementation must account for hospital operational readiness, rural and small provider constraints, technology transition costs, testing needs, and the risk that reporting or standards transitions could create new burdens if not phased and coordinated.

## 3. REGULATORY CONTEXT

- **Specific provisions addressed:** PA-DRUG-MEDICAL; PA-DRUG-PHARMACY; FHIR-IG-REQUIRED; API-ENDPOINT-REPORTING; API-USAGE-METRICS; GENERAL.
- **Regulatory citations mentioned:** CMS-0057-F referenced; no CFR citations mentioned.
- **Standards referenced:** FHIR-based interoperability standards; standardized APIs; existing ANSI transactions; electronic prior authorization; API endpoint and usage metrics.

## 4. DETAILED POSITIONS

**Topic 1: Extending electronic prior authorization to drugs**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DRUG-MEDICAL / PA-DRUG-PHARMACY
- **Position:** Support.
- **Rationale:** Tennessee hospitals experience administrative burden and patient care delays from fragmented PA processes for drugs under medical and pharmacy benefits. Extending CMS-0057-F's framework to drugs would create a more unified and predictable authorization process.
- **Specific request:** Finalize drug ePA requirements using standardized APIs, especially for physician-administered drugs, infusion therapies, oncology treatments, biologics, and other medically necessary therapies.

**Topic 2: Coverage and documentation requirements in the PA API**
- **Provision ID:** FHIR-IG-REQUIRED / PA-DRUG-MEDICAL
- **Position:** Support.
- **Rationale:** Providers spend substantial time identifying payer-specific requirements that are not easily accessible or consistently communicated.
- **Specific request:** Incorporate coverage rules and documentation requirements directly into the Prior Authorization API so providers can view requirements and status earlier in the process.

**Topic 3: Implementation timeline and transition flexibility**
- **Provision ID:** FHIR-IG-REQUIRED / HIPAA-PA-STANDARDS (by implication) / GENERAL
- **Position:** Modify.
- **Rationale:** Hospitals, especially rural hospitals and smaller community providers, face workforce shortages, financial pressures, and technology implementation challenges. Transitioning from existing ANSI transactions to updated electronic standards requires coordination among hospitals, health systems, EHR vendors, clearinghouses, and payers.
- **Specific request:** Maintain flexibility, consider phased implementation, allow a temporary transition period where current transaction standards remain available alongside new standards, and provide sufficient testing before deadlines.

**Topic 4: API endpoint and usage metric reporting**
- **Provision ID:** API-ENDPOINT-REPORTING / API-USAGE-METRICS
- **Position:** Support with caution.
- **Rationale:** Reporting endpoint and usage metrics can help CMS evaluate adoption, efficiency, burden reduction, and communication improvements, but overly broad requirements may create new administrative burdens.
- **Specific request:** Keep reporting requirements targeted and balanced so they do not unintentionally burden providers and payers.

**Topic 5: Reducing manual, fax, and portal workflows**
- **Provision ID:** GENERAL / FHIR-IG-REQUIRED
- **Position:** Support.
- **Rationale:** Manual, fax-based, and portal-based PA workflows create inefficiencies and divert clinical staff from patient care.
- **Specific request:** Use standardized electronic workflows to reduce manual processes and increase operational efficiency.

## 5. SOLICITATION RESPONSES

- **S1/S18/S37:** Supports requiring standardized API-based ePA, while emphasizing operational readiness, phased implementation, testing, and provider constraints.
- **S12:** Identifies technical and operational challenges for hospitals, including technology development, workflow redesign, staff education, and coordination with EHR vendors, clearinghouses, and payers.
- **S21:** Supports drug ePA but asks CMS to consider implementation timelines and readiness, especially for rural/small providers.
- **S23/S29/S34/S35:** Supports API endpoint and usage metric reporting, provided reporting is targeted and balanced to avoid new administrative burden.
- **S44/S46/S47/S53/S54:** Although not directly framed as HIPAA standards, THA addresses transition from existing ANSI transactions to new standards and recommends coexistence/temporary transition, phasing, and testing.

## 6. RECOMMENDATIONS

1. Finalize extension of interoperability and prior authorization requirements to drugs.
2. Require impacted payers to support ePA using standardized APIs.
3. Incorporate coverage rules and documentation requirements directly into the Prior Authorization API.
4. Recognize operational and financial challenges for rural hospitals and smaller community providers.
5. Provide adequate time for technology development, workflow redesign, staff education, and coordination with payer partners.
6. Allow a temporary transition period where current transaction standards remain available alongside new standards.
7. Consider phased implementation where appropriate.
8. Ensure sufficient testing opportunities before full implementation deadlines.
9. Require API endpoint and usage metrics but keep reporting targeted and balanced.
10. Continue collaboration with providers, hospitals, health plans, vendors, and other stakeholders.

## 7. CONCERNS & OBJECTIONS

- **Primary concerns:** Operational readiness, financial and workforce constraints, transition from existing ANSI transactions, insufficient testing, and reporting burden.
- **Potential negative impacts cited:** Disrupted continuity of care, delayed treatment initiation, provider burden, patient confusion, and implementation disruption for rural and smaller providers.
- **Implementation barriers mentioned:** Workforce shortages, financial pressure, technology implementation challenges, EHR vendor coordination, clearinghouse coordination, payer coordination, workflow redesign, and staff education needs.

## 8. SUPPORTING EVIDENCE

- **Data or statistics cited:** THA represents more than 160 healthcare facility members. No additional quantitative data provided.
- **Studies or research referenced:** Not addressed.
- **Examples provided:** Physician-administered drugs, infusion therapies, oncology treatments, biologics, specialty drugs, high-cost medications, time-sensitive therapies, manual/fax/portal workflows, and rural/small hospital implementation constraints.

## 9. IMPACT ASSESSMENT

- **Affected stakeholders:** Tennessee hospitals and health systems, rural hospitals, smaller community providers, patients needing time-sensitive therapies, EHR vendors, clearinghouses, payers, providers, and clinical staff.
- **Economic implications:** Implementation will require technology development, testing, workflow redesign, staff education, and coordination; financial pressures are significant for rural and smaller providers.
- **Technical feasibility:** Feasible with phased implementation, temporary coexistence of current and new standards, and pre-deadline testing.
- **Patient care impact:** Standardized workflows and clearer documentation requirements could improve continuity of care, reduce confusion, and speed access for specialty, oncology, infusion, biologic, and other high-cost therapies.

## 10. SENTIMENT ANALYSIS

- **Overall position:** Supportive with implementation caution.
- **Tone:** Professional, constructive, provider-focused.
- **Priority level:** Medium-high.

## 11. KEY QUOTES

1. "Tennessee hospitals and health systems strongly support CMS's continued efforts to modernize and streamline prior authorization processes." - Context: Overall position.
2. "Extending the interoperability and prior authorization framework established in the CMS Interoperability and Prior Authorization final rule (CMS-0057-F) to include drugs is a logical and necessary next step." - Context: Support for drug ePA expansion.
3. "Many hospitals, particularly rural hospitals and smaller community providers, continue to face workforce shortages, financial pressures, and technology implementation challenges." - Context: Need for implementation flexibility.
4. "Providers may benefit from a temporary transition period in which current transaction standards remain available alongside the new standards." - Context: Transition/coexistence request.

- [x] **IMPLEMENTATION-TIMELINE** - THA requests flexibility, phasing, transition periods, and testing before deadlines.
- [x] **COST-RESOURCES** - Financial pressures, staffing shortages, and implementation costs are central concerns.
- [x] **PROVIDER-BURDEN** - The comment emphasizes administrative burden, manual workflows, and provider inefficiency.
- [ ] **PRIVACY-SECURITY** - Not addressed.
- [ ] **HEALTH-EQUITY** - Rural/smaller providers are discussed, but health equity is not a major framing.
- [x] **TECHNICAL-FEASIBILITY** - THA emphasizes standards transition, testing, technology development, and vendor/clearinghouse coordination.
- [x] **STANDARDS-MATURITY** - The comment addresses updated FHIR-based standards and transition from existing ANSI transactions.
- [x] **PATIENT-ACCESS** - THA focuses on timely access, continuity of care, time-sensitive therapies, and treatment initiation.
- [ ] **REGULATORY-AUTHORITY** - Not addressed.
- [x] **STAKEHOLDER-COORDINATION** - THA asks CMS to coordinate with providers, vendors, payers, clearinghouses, and hospitals.
- [x] **MEDICAL-VS-PHARMACY-BENEFIT** - The comment references fragmented processes for drugs covered under medical and pharmacy benefits.
- [x] **TRANSPARENCY** - Supports improved transparency, coverage rules, documentation expectations, status updates, endpoint/usage metrics.
- [ ] **SMALL-PAYER-IMPACT** - Not addressed.
- [x] **EXISTING-WORKFLOWS** - Focuses on manual, fax-based, portal-based, and ANSI transaction workflows.
- [x] **VENDOR-ECOSYSTEM** - Notes coordination with EHR vendors, clearinghouses, payers, and technology vendors.
